country.comment: Examines the Zona Metropolitana del Valle de México (ZMVM), comprising Ciudad de México (16 delegaciones/alcaldías), 59 municipalities of the Estado de México, and 1 municipality of Hidalgo, with a municipal case study of Ecatepec (Estado de México).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title; PDF p. 2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 6, Footnote 2

effect_estimate.comment: No statistical regression or causal effect size is estimated; quantitative figures are descriptive rates drawn from the 2015 INEGI Intercensal Survey and González (2017), paired with qualitative institutional-historical and newspaper protest analysis.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative / descriptive — no inferential numeric effect estimate reported. Descriptively, 81.39% of the ZMVM population had in-dwelling water access in 2015 while 3 million people lacked drainage and potable water; in the Central Region and Contour 1 no municipality/alcaldía had <98% piped-water availability, whereas >10% lacked piped water in peripheral Contours 3-4, and at least 15 peripheral Estado de México municipalities had <40% in-dwelling water access compared with only 2 of 16 CDMX alcaldías at 40-45% (despite ~30% of ZMVM water originating from the Estado de México). Historically centralized infrastructure prioritizing CDMX, unplanned peripheral urbanization in irregular settlements, incomplete municipal fiscal/technical decentralization, intergovernmental partisan conflict, and clientelist water allocation (reflected in 7 Ecatepec water protests in 2018-2020) drive peripheral water scarcity and supply cuts.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF pp. 9-12, Figures 1-2; PDF pp. 14-16, Table 1; PDF pp. 17-21

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (documented descriptive/institutional association; design ceiling <= 2). Spatial census maps document descriptive center-periphery disparities in piped-water coverage (Figures 1-2) and Table 1 catalogs 7 newspaper-reported water protests in Ecatepec, while causal mechanisms linking partisan clientelism, irregular tenure, and incomplete decentralization to household water deprivation rely largely on secondary literature (e.g., Hernández, 2015; Pineda, 2002; Perló & González, 2009) rather than direct primary observation of administrative processes.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 9-16, Figures 1-2 & Table 1; PDF pp. 17-20

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines irregular land tenure/settlements without legal title (ELIGIBILITY, tenure) and unplanned peripheral growth (planning), core-periphery territorial prioritization of CDMX over Estado de México (service_area), arbitrary and partisan/clientelist allocation and cuts of water supply (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion), citizen participation and water protests vs clientelist intermediation (participation), and fragmented federal/state/municipal/alcaldía jurisdiction, incomplete fiscal decentralization after the 1983 municipalization and 2016 CDMX reform, and partisan intergovernmental conflict across Federal Government, CDMX, CAEM, and municipal SAPASE (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, tenure, planning, service_area, discretion, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes in-dwelling water access (water_access), access to the public piped network vs tanker trucks/pipas (formal_connection), municipal piped-water coverage across concentric rings (service_coverage), electoral/intergovernmental supply cuts and restoration protests (service_continuity), and deficiencies in water quantity/scarcity and potable water quality (service_quantity, service_quality).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Selected because the study is an institutional-historical and neoinstitutional documentary/newspaper study of intergovernmental water governance, municipalization/decentralization, irregular settlements, and partisan clientelism with secondary descriptive census mapping, rather than a primary qualitative fieldwork study (no interviews, focus groups, or ethnography for CASP) or an analytical cross-sectional regression study (JBI).
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 3, Introducción; PDF pp. 12-20

sample_size.comment: No primary household survey or interview sample was collected. Empirical units comprise the 76 ZMVM municipalities/alcaldías mapped using secondary INEGI 2015 Intercensal Survey data and 7 media-documented water protest episodes (May 2018 to September 2020) in the Ecatepec municipal case study.
sample_size.value: 76 municipalities/alcaldías in the Zona Metropolitana del Valle de México (16 CDMX delegaciones/alcaldías, 59 Estado de México municipalities, 1 Hidalgo municipality; 20,892,724 inhabitants in INEGI 2015 descriptive mapping); 1 case-study municipality (Ecatepec) with 7 water protest events (2018-2020 newspaper review)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 6, Footnote 2; PDF pp. 10-11, Figures 1-2; PDF p. 12 & PDF pp. 15-16, Table 1

study_design.comment: Combines historical-institutional analysis of Valley of Mexico water governance and intergovernmental relations with descriptive concentric-ring mapping of INEGI 2015 piped-water lack across ZMVM municipalities/alcaldías and a newspaper review (seguimiento hemerográfico) of 7 water protests in Ecatepec (2018-2020).
study_design.value: Institutional-historical and qualitative case study combining documentary analysis, descriptive spatial mapping of secondary census data (INEGI 2015), and newspaper event tracking (seguimiento hemerográfico) from a neoinstitutional perspective
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 3, Introducción; PDF pp. 10-12; PDF pp. 15-16, Table 1
